card.hook: White marble next to dark water is a great trick: the Oslo Opera House looks like it's sliding straight into the fjord. Stand across the harbour and you get the whole building plus its twin upside down in the water.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Langkaigata waterfront promenade, across the harbour from the Opera House. The Opera House is to the south-east, about 3 minutes on foot away, so face back toward its front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the front of the building, its reflection and a bit of promenade in one shot. Switch to 1x for a tidier, more natural look, and try 2x if your phone has it to pick out the marble slopes and the roofline.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the building, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the white marble keeps its detail instead of glowing flat.
card.best_time: Go in the afternoon, when the sun hits the front of the building. Calm weather gives you the clearest reflection, so take a few frames in case ripples spoil one.
card.selfie_here: Head up the sloped ramp toward the roof and find the big glass window; one visitor treated it as a 'window selfie' spot, with the glass and its reflections behind them. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the building over your shoulder. The front plaza (Kirsten Flagstads plass) is a simpler backup, with the glass-and-aluminium façade behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on Langkaigata to face back toward the front of the Opera House so its reflection shows in the water, and stand a few steps in front of them on the promenade.
card.rules_and_safety: The roof is normally open to walk on, but sections can close for safety or maintenance, and the marble may be restricted in snow or ice, so check the official site before you go. One visitor reported someone slipping on the exterior ramp, so take care on drizzly days.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the building and its reflection look like a perfect mirror image, with the water's edge sitting on the lower gridline.
card.good_to_know: The Oslo Opera House is the home of the Norwegian National Opera and Ballet. It sits in the Bjørvika neighbourhood at the head of the Oslofjord, was designed by Snøhetta and opened on 12 April 2008. Its sloping white surfaces are covered in Carrara marble and white granite, and the roof slopes down to ground level so you can walk up it.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Langkaigata waterfront promenade, across the harbour from the Opera House. The Opera House is to the south-east, about 3 minutes on foot away, so face back toward its front.

card.hook: Here's a fun one: old stone fortress on your side of the water, a tall, tilted, very modern museum on the other. Old and new in one shot, and the harbour in the middle keeps the peace.
card.stand_here: Stand in the grounds of Akershus Festning and face east across the harbour, where MUNCH sits on the waterfront. Keep the view over the water clear so nothing blocks the line between you and the museum.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to see the whole scene, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to bring the museum closer. MUNCH looks small from across the water at 1x. Use 0.5x only if you want lots of harbour and sky.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the museum, then slide darker a touch if the sky is bright, so the building doesn't turn into a silhouette.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or early evening is likely your best bet, because the sun is behind you and lights up the museum's face. Soft, clear light after sunrise or before sunset works well too.
card.selfie_here: Climb the white marble slope of the Oslo Opera House roof toward the top. MUNCH is in view to the south-east from up there, so use the front camera and turn so the museum is over your shoulder. I can't promise the angle is perfect, so check the frame and shuffle until it works.
card.ask_someone: For a wider shot, ask a passer-by to step back as far as they can from the canal bank beside the museum, while you stand at the water's edge so the building and its reflection fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: One visitor guide says selfie sticks aren't allowed at MUNCH, and another says no flash inside. The Opera House marble can be slippery when wet, icy or snowy, and parts of the roof may be closed in winter. Check the official site for visiting rules and tickets before you go.
card.challenge: Take three shots at different zooms, then pick the winner, the one where the museum and the harbour feel perfectly balanced.
card.good_to_know: MUNCH is dedicated to Edvard Munch and holds almost 28,000 artworks. They moved here from the old museum at Tøyen. King Harald V opened the new building on 22 October 2021.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the grounds of Akershus Festning and face east across the harbour, where MUNCH sits on the waterfront. Keep the view over the water clear so nothing blocks the line between you and the museum.

card.hook: Here's a fun twist: the star of this spot is a building that's about 103 m across, built just to shelter three Viking burial ships. It's big, calm and very patient, which makes it an easy subject for your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Viking Ship Museum on Bygdøy, right where the phone icon sits on the map, so there's no walk once you arrive. Then step back from the entrance and face the building, so the whole front fits in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x if you're close to the walls, then switch to 1x as you step back for a calmer, truer-looking view. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for details like rooflines and the entrance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the roof and walls with them, so the long walls stay straight and the building looks proud, not wonky.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters a building like this. Early in the day also tends to be quieter.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie outside at the museum front, with the Bygdøy garden behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the museum over your shoulder. Nothing names an exact standing point, so pick a spot where the building fills the background.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the approach in front of the entrance and frame the whole façade, while you pose in front of the building.
card.rules_and_safety: The museum is temporarily closed until 2027, so interior photos aren't possible right now. Check the official site before you go to see what's open.
card.challenge: Get the whole building in one shot with the walls dead straight on the gridlines and a little strip of ground in front. Bonus points for a sky with some personality.
card.good_to_know: The museum shelters three Viking-era burial ships, from Tune, Gokstad and Oseberg. The Oseberg ship is the best known, and it came from the largest known ship burial in the world. Arnstein Arneberg won the architectural contest, the Oseberg hall was ready in 1926, and the last hall was finished in 1957 after delays partly due to the Second World War.

card.hook: Picture a 17 m granite tower made of people climbing over each other, and you're standing right at the bottom, neck tilted back. The Monolith is the one spot in Vigeland Park where looking up is the whole point.
card.stand_here: Stand at the foot of the granite column on the Monolith plateau and shoot upward. The subject lies to the south-east of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x from close to the base to squeeze the whole column in. Switch to 1x for a calmer view, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out single figures near the top.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and keep the column on a vertical line, then tap the column and drag the brightness slider down a touch so the sky stays blue instead of washing out.
card.best_time: Early morning or late evening light is best. An early weekday visit is likely to be quieter around the column.
card.selfie_here: Try the bridge near the Angry Boy (Sinnataggen). Face back toward the Main Gate so the Monolith at the far end of the central path should be behind you, and use the front camera at 0.5x if you can. The column will look small from that far away, so think of it as a 'yes, I was here' shot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back from you on the bridge and shoot from a low angle, so the Monolith shows up behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photography is unrestricted in the park, but commercial photography and film need a permit from the park administration. Paths can be icy and the open lawns are cold and windy, so wear shoes with grip and a warm hat and gloves if you linger at the Monolith.
card.challenge: Walk all the way round the column and find the side where the figures look the most dramatic, then take one shot from there.
card.good_to_know: Building began in 1924, and this is described as the largest sculpture park in the world made by a single artist. Most figures show ordinary moments like running, wrestling, dancing and hugging, so you can see the story in a single frame. It gets one to two million visitors a year, so a patient wait for a gap pays off.

card.hook: Picture a thick stone wall in the corner of your phone and a whole sparkling harbour filling the rest. That's the southern ramparts at Akershus, and guides often call this walkway the most-photographed spot on the site.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, on the southern ramparts (festningsvollene), and face the harbour. You'll have the fortress walls close in front of you, Aker Brygge stretching away to the west and the fjord opening out to the south.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the wall, harbour and sky in together. Then try 1x for a calmer, less stretched look. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) picks out boats or the Aker Brygge buildings across the water.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, keep the horizon level, and put a stretch of wall in the bottom corner so the picture feels anchored.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is the sweet spot, when the sun sits in the west and lights up the water.
card.selfie_here: Find one of the cannons along the outer grounds and pose beside it with the castle walls behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to squeeze in more wall, and hold the phone a little high. The stationary guard post at the fortress entrance is another popular tourist photo stop, so check the map for where it is.
card.ask_someone: Wait on the Stranden harbour promenade below the fortress walls and ask a passer-by to take your photo from there, with the stone walls and towers rising above you.
card.rules_and_safety: Some of the best views are from unfenced edges, so keep well clear of ledges and drops when you pose. The grounds are free to walk, but the museum and some inner areas charge admission, and side gates can close early in winter, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the stone wall sits in the corner and the horizon is dead straight, then see if your travel buddy can spot the Aker Brygge buildings in it.
card.good_to_know: Building is thought to have begun in the late 1290s under King Haakon V. After a great fire in 1624, King Christian IV moved the city closer to the fortress, and the castle was remodelled with Italian-inspired bastions. It has survived every siege, and today it's also the prime minister's temporary office.

card.hook: A balsa-wood raft that sailed from Peru to Polynesia in 1947 now has its own building on Oslo's Bygdøy peninsula. Your photo is the 'yes, I found it' shot, with the name, the entrance and a bit of the surroundings.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Kon-Tiki Museum on Bygdøy, where the phone icon on the map sits right at the museum itself. Face the front entrance and step back until the whole front fits in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole front of the building. If you can't step back far enough, try 0.5x, but keep the building away from the edges so it doesn't look stretched. Then go to 2x for a closer shot of the entrance or the sign.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building's edges with them so the walls stay straight, then tap the building and slide it a touch darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Daytime in good, even light is the easiest for a clear shot of the building. Early or late in the day the light is softer, but check the museum's own times before you plan around it.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the Thor Heyerdahl statue just outside the entrance and turn so the museum is behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more of the building, and hold the phone level so the walls stay straight.

card.good_to_know: The museum was built to house the Kon-Tiki, the raft Thor Heyerdahl sailed from Peru to Polynesia in 1947. card.hook: Most museums keep the exhibit inside the building. At the Fram Museum, the building was made around the exhibit: a whole polar ship, sitting indoors like the world's most impressive parked car.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Fram Museum on Bygdøy, right where the phone icon on the map sits. Then walk to the outside of the building and pick a spot with enough room to fit its long outline into the frame.
card.zoom: Outside, try zoom 0.5x to squeeze in the whole front, then 1x for a tighter shot. Inside, zoom 0.5x is your friend for the hull and rigging, 1x suits the original interior details, and zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) gets you close to rigging or signs.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line up the roof and walls with them so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Outside, pick a bright but softly lit part of the day. Inside, go whenever it's quietest so other visitors stay out of your shots.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and step back until the building fills the space behind you. Try zoom 0.5x to fit more of it in, and keep it over your shoulder so you're not hiding it.
card.rules_and_safety: Photo rules inside the museum may vary, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Shoot along the hull inside and see if you can make the ship look as huge as it feels.
card.good_to_know: Fram was designed and built by Colin Archer to Fridtjof Nansen's specifications and financed in 1891. The museum opened on 20 May 1936 and also honours Otto Sverdrup and Roald Amundsen. Next door, Gjøa has its own building. It was the first vessel to sail through the Northwest Passage, which Amundsen and a crew of six completed in 1906.

card.hook: Here's a funny thing: the best view of Aker Brygge isn't from Aker Brygge. The wharf is busy, so walk a little way off and let the whole waterfront show itself.
card.stand_here: Walk a short stroll south-west along the water towards Tjuvholmen, near the Astrup Fearnley Museum of Modern Art. Stand on the pier at the Tjuvholmen end, then turn round and face back to the north-east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the pavilions, the water and the waterfront in together. Then try 2x to pick out the buildings and lights, or 0.5x if you want more foreground and sky.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the horizon level, and let the water fill the lower part of the frame so the reflections do some of the work.
card.best_time: Go for blue hour, the 30 minutes after sunset, when the lights come on and the sky still has some colour.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera, tap 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold your phone a little higher than usual. Keep the waterfront behind you, over your shoulder, so it fits in with you.
card.rules_and_safety: The pier and waterfront are free public spaces. If you plan to go inside any building or museum, check the official site first.
card.challenge: Get the horizon dead level on the gridlines, then see how many light reflections you can count in the water.
card.good_to_know: Until 1982 this was the Akers Mekaniske Verksted shipyard, and before 1854 the area was known as Holmen. Several of the big workshop halls were rebuilt as shops and restaurants, and the first stage of the new district was finished in 1986. Today it draws around 12 million visitors a year.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk a short stroll south-west along the water towards Tjuvholmen, near the Astrup Fearnley Museum of Modern Art. Stand on the pier at the Tjuvholmen end, then turn round and face back to the north-east.

card.hook: Walk up Karl Johans gate and the whole street seems to point at one calm, pale building, so you can't really miss it. The fun part is making it look as good on your phone as it does in real life.
card.stand_here: Head for Slottsplassen, the forecourt in front of the Royal Palace, and face the palace facade. Try standing a little to the left side of the forecourt rather than dead centre, so you get a slight angle and a less flat picture.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the full facade with the statue of Karl Johan in front. If you're close and the building won't fit, tap 0.5x. Use 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the colonnade or the balcony.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the palace's horizontal edges with them, so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Mornings and afternoons can both look good here, so try both if you can. If you want the changing of the guard at 1:30pm (it's daily), arrive about 10 minutes early to grab a good spot.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on Slottsplassen, on the open square in front of the main facade. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the palace over your shoulder so it fills the background. For a softer portrait with trees around you, try the lawns or paths in the side gardens of Slottsparken, next to the palace.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand a good way back on Karl Johans gate, facing the palace, while you stand in front of it, so the whole building is framed at the top of the avenue with you in front.
card.rules_and_safety: The grounds are free and open to the public, but photography isn't allowed inside the palace. Check the official site before you go for tours and any current closures or rules.
card.challenge: Put the statue of Karl Johan low in your frame with the palace right behind him, and see if you can make it look like he's guarding the place.
card.good_to_know: The palace is the official residence of the Norwegian monarch. It was built for Charles XIV John, the French-born king of Norway and Sweden, and the architect was Hans Linstow. The foundation stone was laid in 1825, the roof went on in 1836 and the interiors were finished in the late 1840s. The Palace Park around it is about 22 hectares, so there's plenty of room to step back for a wider view.

card.hook: Picture a wide avenue running straight uphill to a yellow palace, with nothing but open sky above it. That's Karl Johans gate, and it's about as easy a photo as Oslo gets.
card.stand_here: Stand on the front plaza of Stortinget (the Parliament building) and face up the avenue towards the yellow Royal Palace. The street on the map is a short step to the east, behind you as you face the palace.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole avenue and the palace in one go. Try zoom 2x to bring the palace closer and make the street look more squeezed together, or zoom 0.5x if you want the plaza and the buildings around you too.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the middle of the avenue on the centre vertical line, and hold the phone level so the street leads the eye up to the palace.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when the sun lights up the front of the palace. If people keep walking through your shot, wait a moment or take a Live Photo and pick the cleanest frame afterwards.
card.selfie_here: Try the steps of the National Theatre, in the middle of the street. A travel guide calls them a classic photo spot, so switch to the front camera and put the avenue behind you. For a bigger view, the slope above the palace park lets you fit Karl Johans gate behind you as it runs down below.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Stortinget plaza facing you while you stand in front of the Parliament, so the avenue runs away behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Karl Johans gate and the Stortinget plaza are open public space. On 17 May and during Christmas market periods, access and the look of the street can change, so check the official site first if you're visiting then.
card.challenge: Take the same shot twice, once at zoom 1x and once at zoom 2x, and see which one makes the palace look like it's sitting at the end of a very long hill.
card.good_to_know: The western part of the street was built in the 1840s to link the new palace with the rest of the city. It was named Karl Johans gate in 1852, after King Charles III John, who was also King Charles XIV John of Sweden. When Stortinget was finished in 1866, two separate streets were joined under that one name, and the king's statue in front of the palace was added in 1875.

card.hook: Some buildings fuss. This one doesn't. The National Museum is a big, calm block of pale stone and dark metal, with clean lines and plain surfaces that make your phone look like a pro.
card.stand_here: Start right at the phone icon on the map, at the museum itself. Then step out to the harbour-side approach and back away from the building until the Light Hall's granite and brick facade fits in the frame, with the harbour around you.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for the whole front. If you're close and it won't fit, drop to zoom 0.5x. Go to zoom 2x to pick out the granite, brick and metal panels.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them, so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Soft daylight suits the stone and metal best, and overcast skies give calm, even colours. Low sun can add some warmth, so try a wide shot and a close shot whatever the light.
card.selfie_here: Head to the pier outside the museum, next to the giant bronze 'Mother' sculpture, which is a popular photo spot. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and hold it a bit low, so the museum fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Universitetsgata, across from the main facade, so the whole building fits in the frame, while you pose in front of the entrance.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are allowed in the exhibition rooms, but flash isn't. Temporary exhibitions may set their own limits, and restricted areas have 'No Photography' signs.
card.challenge: Stand in the middle of the front for a symmetrical shot of the bronze-and-glass facade and see if you can catch the sky's colour in the metal panels.
card.good_to_know: The National Museum (Nasjonalmuseet) is Norway's state collection of art, architecture and design. It opened in June 2022 on the site of the old Oslo West Station, at Vestbanen on the edge of Aker Brygge. The collection has over 400,000 works, including the first copy of Edvard Munch's The Scream from 1893.

card.hook: Count the towers: there are two, but they're not twins. One is 63 metres and the other is 66, and the chunky red brick below them looks great on a phone screen.
card.stand_here: Stand in Rådhusplassen, the open square in front of the main facade. From here the building lies to the north-east, so face that way and step back until both towers fit.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the whole facade and both towers in one shot. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look, then try 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) for the reliefs and the tops of the towers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line a tower up with an upright line and keep your phone level, because tilting it back makes the towers lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and fewer people, and the brick looks warmer in low sun. Skip 10 December if you want a quiet square.
card.selfie_here: Take it on Rådhusplassen, facing the red-brick building with the twin towers behind you. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) and hold it a little low so both towers fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a full-length photo, ask someone to shoot from the harbour-side quay by Rådhusbryggene while you stand on the quay with the twin towers filling the background.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos for personal use are generally fine in public areas, but there can be restrictions during ceremonies or official events. The City Hall is closed on some days, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a Werenskiold relief on the square side, zoom in on one scene from the Poetic Edda, and see if a friend can guess the story.
card.good_to_know: Oslo City Hall was built between 1931 and 1950, with a pause during the Second World War. It was designed by Arnstein Arneberg and Magnus Poulsson. The bricks are bigger than was usual in the 1930s, closer to medieval brick, which gives the walls that chunky look. The Nobel Peace Prize ceremony is held here every 10 December, so expect crowds and possible closures then.

card.hook: Most parliaments tuck the debating chamber away in the middle. Norway's Storting pushes it out front in one big curve, which is great news for your photos.
card.stand_here: Stand on Eidsvolls plass, the open forecourt right in front of the Storting, and face the main façade. From here the building lies to the south-east.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x to fit the whole yellow-brick front with the square around it. Try zoom 2x for the lions and the curved middle section, and zoom 0.5x only if you want lots of sky and ground (the edges can stretch).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the building up so its base sits on a horizontal line, then keep your phone level so the long lines stay straight.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to the brickwork than harsh midday sun. Near sunset, wander over to Stortingsparken for the building with a colourful sky behind it.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside one of the two lion statues on the ramp up to the entrance. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and let the pale yellow façade rise over your shoulder (one guide rates it as a strong photo spot, so have a look on site). Eidsvolls plass also works if you want the whole building behind you.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the forecourt in front of the façade and ask a passer-by to stand back on the square facing you, so the whole building fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay outside for your photos, as indoor photography is restricted in working parliamentary areas. On a visitor tour, photos are permitted but video is forbidden.
card.challenge: Go low by the lions and get a lion, the entrance and the curved middle all in one shot.
card.good_to_know: The Storting is Norway's parliament, designed by Swedish architect Emil Victor Langlet and taken into use on 5 March 1866. The two stone lions on the approach, known as Løvebakken (the Lions Hill), have been there since 1865. The pale grey granite base and yellow walls give a calm, even colour that phones handle well.

card.hook: You'll probably hear Oslo Cathedral before you've lined up your shot, because the carillon in the tower rings every hour and quarter-hour. Let it be your cue to look up at that tall bronze-steepled tower.
card.stand_here: Stand in Stortorvet square, across the street from the cathedral's main facade, and face east. The tower and the pale yellow brick front should fill your view. If the statue of Christian IV is there, he'll be in front of you, looking up at the church.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the tower, the facade and the statue all fit in one frame. Go to 0.5x for the whole tower plus lots of foreground, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the tower top and its details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and hold your phone level so the tower stands straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives the nicest light, especially for the street-level view from Karl Johans gate. Whenever you come, it's worth waiting for the carillon.
card.selfie_here: Try the park at Eidsvolls plass, just behind the cathedral. It's quieter than the street, so turn your back to the church and use the front camera at 0.5x to keep the cathedral over your shoulder. The square at Stortorvet works too.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the plaza across the street by the statue of King Christian IV (if it's still there) while you stand with the church behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos inside are generally fine for personal use, but skip the flash, especially during services or prayer. The cathedral is a working church, so ask before photographing people. Some entrances have steps and the stone floors are uneven, so wear comfy shoes.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the statue is low in the frame and the tower rises straight up behind it, like the statue is pointing you to the sky.
card.good_to_know: This is the third cathedral in Oslo's history. The current building went up between 1694 and 1697 and was consecrated in November 1697. It was rebuilt in 1848-1850 and reopened in April 2010 after a long renovation. Prince Haakon's wedding was held here in 2001.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Stortorvet square, across the street from the cathedral's main facade, and face east. The tower and the pale yellow brick front should fill your view. If the statue of Christian IV is there, he'll be in front of you, looking up at the church.

card.hook: Picture a dark, tarred timber church with steep roofs stacked up like layers of a cake, sitting calmly on a green lawn. That's the Gol stave church, and it's the star of the museum grounds.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, outside the Gol stave church, and walk slowly round its tarred walls and carved portal. Face the church so the dark timber and the green grounds fill your picture.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole church in. Go to zoom 0.5x when you're close to the walls and want the full height of the roofs, then zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for the carved portal.
card.make_it_pop: The walls are very dark, so tap the wall and slide the brightness a touch darker if the sky starts to wash out.
card.best_time: One guide says morning light works best. The carvings also tend to look best outside in open shade rather than in the dim interior.
card.selfie_here: Head to the entrance of the Gol stave church, on the open-air grounds at Bygdøy. Use the front camera, turn so the doorway is behind you, and try zoom 0.5x to squeeze more of the church in over your shoulder.

card.challenge: Take a slow lap of the church and find your favourite roof line, then snap it from three different corners and pick the winner.
card.good_to_know: The church dates from the 13th century and joined the museum in 1907. It's one of five medieval buildings on site, and part of a group of relocated buildings recognised as the world's first open-air museum. The museum was founded in 1894 and opened to the public in 1901.

card.hook: Plot twist: the grand yellow building on Oslo's City Hall Square wasn't built for peace at all. It was built for trains, and you can still see it in the long, handsome front.

card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the building up with the horizontal lines so the long front doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Evening is a good bet, as the plaza is likely to be quieter then. Try night mode and hold your phone steady against a railing or your body.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Aker Brygge waterfront on the harbour side and turn so the museum's front facade is behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the building over your shoulder. card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Rådhusplassen at the museum end with the building in view, while you pose in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is open public space, but the museum charges admission and temporary exhibitions may restrict photography, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take three quick frames as you stroll across the square and see how the building, the fjord and City Hall swap places.
card.good_to_know: Architect Georg Andreas Bull drew this building in 1872 as the West railway station, and trains stopped using it in 1989. The Nobel Peace Center opened here in 2005 and gets around 250,000 visitors a year. Oslo City Hall, just next door, hosts the Peace Prize ceremony every 10 December.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Rådhusplassen (City Hall Square) at the end nearest the Nobel Peace Center, with City Hall behind you. Face the yellow building across the open square.

card.hook: Picture a giant steel slide sticking out of the forest, with tiny walkers on the road below it. That's Holmenkollbakken, and it looks even bigger when you're standing under it.
card.stand_here: Stand on Kongeveien, on the stretch past the run-out end of the jump, on the main road back toward the metro. Face the jump so it runs up in front of you, with the steel tower rising above the trees.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x, because you're close and the jump is long and tall. If you can step back far enough, switch to 1x, or try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the tower against the trees.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and hold your phone upright so the tower stands straight, then tap the tower and slide the brightness a little darker so the pale sky doesn't wash out the steel.
card.best_time: Soft light early or late in the day works well. A bright overcast day is good too, because the steel and trees show clearly without harsh shadows.
card.selfie_here: Try the forest by Holmenkollen Chapel, where the jump rises behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone allows, and keep the jump over your shoulder. The Ski Museum terrace is another spot for a selfie with the jump in the frame, and one guide suggests sunset there.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the road back toward Holmenkollen metro station, where the path passes the very end of the jump run (the Kollentrollet troll sculpture is across the road), to take your photo with the jump rising behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Kongeveien is an open public road, but the area can be closed or restricted during competitions and events, so check the official site before you go. Photography is generally allowed in public areas. Watch your footing on the stairs around the arena, especially in winter.
card.challenge: Make the slope run corner to corner like a big diagonal, with the tower at the top and nobody walking through the frame.
card.good_to_know: The hill is rated HS134 and can hold 70,000 spectators. It hosted the 1952 Winter Olympics and several Nordic World Ski Championships. Skiing events have been held here since 1892, but the whole jump was torn down and rebuilt between 2008 and 2010, so it's a modern jump on a very old site.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Kongeveien, on the stretch past the run-out end of the jump, on the main road back toward the metro. Face the jump so it runs up in front of you, with the steel tower rising above the trees.

card.hook: A giant glass sail at the end of a little peninsula: that's the Astrup Fearnley Museum's roof, and it's hard to miss. Line it up right and you get Aker Brygge and Oslo City Hall in the same shot, so the photo says "Oslo" without any caption.
card.stand_here: Head for the phone icon on the map, right at the museum on the Tjuvholmen tip, and face the roof so you can catch its sweep up close. For a wider view, walk to Strandpromenaden on the fjord side and look back at the museum.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole roof with the waterfront and City Hall behind it. If you're close and the roof won't fit, drop to 0.5x. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the roof's lines against City Hall.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the roof's sweeping line on an upper line and let the fjord fill the bottom third, keeping the horizon level.
card.best_time: Go when the light is soft, in the morning or later in the afternoon. Glass and water both bounce a lot of light, so bright midday sun can wash the picture out.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside a sculpture on the grass in Tjuvholmen Sculpture Park, next to the museum, and turn so the museum's facade is behind you. Use the front camera, or 0.5x if you want more of the building in. On Strandpromenaden you can also back up along the boardwalk until the museum sits behind you against the water.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the footbridge that connects Tjuvholmen to the mainland to frame you with the museum and the Opera House in the distance.
card.rules_and_safety: The museum charges admission, and the rooftop terrace and glass bridge are inside, so these views are all from outside. Keep kids and luggage close on the narrow piers, because bikes and scooters sometimes pass closely.
card.challenge: Wait for a few walkers to stroll along the promenade, then snap the roof with one of them in the lower corner to show how big it really is.
card.good_to_know: The museum sits on the tip of Tjuvholmen in central Oslo, beside the Aker Brygge waterfront. Its sail-shaped glass roof is the first thing you notice. From the sculpture park, you can also see Akershus Fortress across the bay behind the museum.

card.hook: Two famous playwrights stand guard at the door of this theatre, and they never once move out of your shot. That makes the National Theatre one of the easier fronts in Oslo to get right.
card.stand_here: Stand in Johanne Dybwads plass, in front of the main facade, between the Ibsen and Bjørnson statues. Face the theatre so the whole neo-baroque front fits in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole facade. If you can't step back far enough, tap 0.5x. For a close-up of one statue or the entrance, try 2x or 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the central entrance with the middle of the frame so the building stands up straight.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is a good bet for the stone and the statues. Flat, overcast midday light can make the statues look duller.
card.selfie_here: Go up the theatre's front steps by the entrance, next to the Ibsen and Bjørnson statues, and turn so the facade is behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone offers it, to fit more of the building over your shoulder. For a leafier backdrop, Studenterlunden park, by the fountain beside Nationaltheatret station, shows the theatre behind the greenery.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in Stortingsparken and frame you so the Ibsen statue and the theatre entrance are visible behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine in public areas and gardens, but not during performances. Inside the auditoriums photography is generally not allowed during performances. The lobby may allow photos, so check the signs or ask staff.
card.challenge: Catch one statue at the edge of the frame with the whole theatre behind it, and keep the building dead straight. Take a few shots in case people walk through.
card.good_to_know: The theatre gave its first performance on 1 September 1899, but its roots go back to the Christiania Theatre, founded in 1829. The opening programme included Ibsen's An Enemy of the People and Bjørnson's Sigurd Jorsalfar. Henrik Bull designed the building, and it sits between the Royal Palace and the Parliament, so it's easy to fit into a walk around the centre.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Johanne Dybwads plass, in front of the main facade, between the Ibsen and Bjørnson statues. Face the theatre so the whole neo-baroque front fits in the frame.
